reason: The sources provide enough surprising facts about Barnard 68 to support a 45-second script with more than 10 verified multi-source claims.
story: Floating in the southern constellation Ophiuchus just 400 light-years away sits Barnard 68, an ink-black void so opaque it looks like a gaping hole in the universe. Discovered by American astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard in 1919, this molecular cloud is a Bok globule measuring about half a light-year across. It is so dense that out of a trillion photons of yellow light shot through its center, only a single one makes it to the other side. Not a single foreground star mars its darkness, and its interior plummets to a freezing 10 Kelvin, making it colder than Pluto and causing gases to freeze onto its dust grains. Astronomers using the Very Large Telescope discovered that this starless stellar nursery is currently jiggling like Jell-O as it balances internal pressure against gravity, on the verge of collapsing to spark a brand new star.
angle: Barnard 68 is so dense that out of a trillion photons of yellow light shot through its center, only one makes it to the other side.

claims.claim: Barnard 68 is located in the southern constellation Ophiuchus.
The cloud is situated at a distance of about 400 to 500 light-years from Earth.
American astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard added the nebula to his catalog in 1919.
Not a single foreground star is observed in front of the cloud.
The temperature of the cloud is approximately 10 Kelvin.
The mass of Barnard 68 is about twice that of the Sun.
It is classified as a Bok globule.
Charles Lada reported that the cloud is vibrating or jiggling.
The cloud measures roughly half a light-year or 5 light-months across.
Bart Bok and Edith Reilly suggested in 1947 that such globules could collapse and form a star.
The cloud's expanded catalog was published posthumously in 1927.

disputed: The exact distance is stated as about 407 light-years in S1 and S3, around 500 light-years in S2, and 300 to 400 light-years in S4; a script should use a general range around 400 light-years.
